plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 5: Stereochemistry at Tetrahedral Centers
plan.contextChunk: This figure pairs a flat structural drawing with a three-dimensional model of the same molecule, both cut by a horizontal plane. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" sit one above the other, joined by a vertical bond. The upper carbon bears an "H" above it on a dashed bond, an "HO" group at the left in magenta on a bold wedge, and a "CO2H" group at the right in green. The lower carbon repeats that arrangement flipped vertically: "HO" again at the left and "CO2H" at the right, but its "H" now points downward on a dashed bond. A pale blue parallelogram drawn edge-on slices horizontally between the two carbons, labeled "Symmetry plane". On the right the molecule appears as a ball-and-stick model, two dark gray carbons stacked vertically, each carrying a small blue sphere, a red oxygen with a second red sphere beyond it, and a branching green group, with an identical pale blue plane passing between them. Running the plane through both depictions asks the reader to check one half against the other. Because the halves are reflections, the molecule proves superimposable on its own mirror image despite having two chirality centers, the situation that defines a meso compound.

elements: Left panel (2D structure): upper carbon lettered 'C' and lower carbon lettered 'C', stacked vertically
Vertical plain bond joining the two 'C' letters
Upper carbon: dashed bond pointing up to a blue 'H' label
Upper carbon: bold wedge pointing left to magenta 'HO' label
Upper carbon: plain bond pointing right to green 'CO2H' label
Lower carbon: dashed bond pointing down to a blue 'H' label
Lower carbon: bold wedge pointing left to magenta 'HO' label
Lower carbon: plain bond pointing right to green 'CO2H' label
Pale blue parallelogram drawn edge-on, slicing horizontally between the two carbons of the 2D structure
Black text label 'Symmetry plane' to the right of the 2D plane
Right panel (ball-and-stick model): upper dark-gray carbon sphere and lower dark-gray carbon sphere, stacked vertically and bonded by a light-gray cylinder
Upper carbon: small pale-blue hydrogen sphere on a short bond (pointing down-right toward viewer)
Upper carbon: red oxygen sphere up-left with a second smaller red sphere (hydroxyl H) beyond it
Upper carbon: green carboxyl carbon sphere up-right, branching to two further green oxygen spheres and a small green hydrogen sphere
Lower carbon: small pale-blue hydrogen sphere (pointing up-right toward viewer, mirrored)
Lower carbon: red oxygen sphere down-left with a second smaller red sphere beyond it
Lower carbon: green carboxyl group branching down-right, mirroring the upper one
Light-gray cylindrical bonds between all spheres
Pale blue transparent plane passing horizontally between the two model carbons, perpendicular to the central C–C bond

interactions.teaches: The same internal mirror plane can be found in the flat line drawing and in the real 3D geometry — the two depictions describe one molecule, not two arguments.
interactions.label: Representation

interactions.teaches: Every substituent on the top stereocenter has an exact mirror partner on the bottom one, so the two centers have opposite configurations and their handedness cancels.
Rotating the ball-and-stick model shows the mirror relationship holds in three dimensions, not just in the drawing's projection.
Reflecting the top half through the plane lands it exactly on the bottom half — the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image, i.e. meso and achiral despite two chirality centers.
interactions.label: Reflect top half through the plane

demo_steps.title: The flat drawing
demo_steps.narration: Two stereocenters stacked vertically: each carries HO on a wedge to the left and CO2H to the right, but the H's point in opposite directions. A pale blue plane slices between them.

demo_steps.title: Same molecule in 3D
demo_steps.narration: The ball-and-stick model shows the same arrangement: gray carbons, a small blue H, a red OH, and a green CO2H on each center, cut by the same horizontal plane.

demo_steps.title: Check group against group
demo_steps.narration: Click HO, H, or CO2H on the upper center; its mirror partner below lights up. Every substituent is matched across the plane.

demo_steps.title: Fold it over
demo_steps.narration: Reflecting the top half through the plane superimposes it on the bottom half — the internal mirror makes this meso compound achiral.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Meso tartaric acid, HO2C–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–CO2H. World scale: central C–C bond 1.6 units, drawn vertically along +Y with the upper carbon at (0, 0.8, 0) and lower at (0, -0.8, 0). Symmetry plane is a horizontal parallelogram in the y=0 plane, ~5 units wide (X) × 2 units deep (Z), pale blue #b9dff5 at ~45% opacity, edges slightly darker; it is perpendicular to the C–C bond and extends beyond the molecule on both sides. Upper carbon substituents (bond length 1.1): OH oxygen up-left at (-0.9, 1.4, 0.15) with its hydroxyl H beyond at (-1.5, 1.05, 0.3); H (small, 0.45× radius) down-right toward viewer at (0.55, 0.45, 0.85); carboxyl carbon up-right at (0.95, 1.4, -0.1), branching to two oxygens at (1.9, 1.15, 0.1) and (0.95, 2.4, -0.3) plus a small acid H. Lower carbon substituents are the exact mirror images through y=0 (negate Y of every upper-half position). Colors: carbon dark gray #4b5058; stereocenter hydrogens pale blue #7cc0e8; hydroxyl oxygen and its hydrogen red/dark red #b23225 and #8f231a; entire CO2H branch rendered green #3fbf5c (matching the green CO2H label in the 2D panel); bonds light gray #c9ced4 cylinders of radius 0.09, with a glossy specular highlight on each sphere. Sphere radii: C 0.38, O 0.34, green carboxyl atoms 0.34, H 0.20. 2D panel (shown in the same scene, offset to screen-left by ~4.5 units, drawn flat facing the camera in the XY plane): two black 'C' letters at (-4.5, 0.55) and (-4.5, -0.55); vertical plain bond between them; upper C has a short dashed vertical bond up to blue 'H' (#1f8fc2) at (-4.5, 1.25), a bold solid wedge left to magenta 'HO' (#d4197f) at (-5.5, 0.9), a plain bond right to green 'CO2H' (#127a4a) at (-3.4, 0.9); lower C mirrors this with the dashed bond and 'H' pointing down. A pale blue edge-on parallelogram at y=0 spans x from -5.6 to -3.6, with black text 'Symmetry plane' to its right at (-2.6, 0). Highlight color for clicked/partner groups: warm yellow glow #ffd24d outline.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the 3D model from THREE.SphereGeometry + CylinderGeometry grouped per substituent so a whole group (OH, H, CO2H) can be highlighted as a unit; give each group a userData tag {half:'top'|'bottom', group:'OH'|'H'|'CO2H'} so a click finds its mirror partner by matching group and flipping half. Plane: PlaneGeometry rotated -PI/2 about X, MeshBasicMaterial transparent, depthWrite false, side DoubleSide, rendered after the molecule to avoid z-fighting. 2D panel drawn as CanvasTexture sprites/planes (or HTML overlay aligned to the canvas) so the colored labels and bold-wedge/dashed-bond typography match the source; wedge as a filled triangle, dashed bond as a stack of short line segments. Overlay mode fades the 2D panel to ~35% opacity behind/beside the model rather than removing it. Reflect animation: lerp a clone of the top-half group through a scale(1,-1,1) mirror matrix over ~1.5 s, ghosting it in translucent cyan so the learner sees it settle exactly onto the bottom half; add a brief 'superimposable' flash on completion. Orbit limited to ±60° elevation so the plane never becomes exactly edge-on-invisible; soft directional key light + ambient fill for the glossy ball-and-stick look.

authoredContext:
The 2R,3S and 2S,3R structures are identical because the molecule has a plane of symmetry and is therefore achiral. The symmetry plane cuts through the C2–C3 bond, making one half of the molecule a mirror image of the other half (the figure). Because of the plane of symmetry, the molecule is achiral, despite the fact that it has two chirality centers. Such compounds, which are achiral, yet contain chirality centers, are called meso compounds (me-zo). Thus, tartaric acid exists in three stereoisomeric forms: two enantiomers and one meso form.

A symmetry plane through the C2–C3 bond of meso-tartaric acid makes the molecule achiral.

The wedge-dash structure and ball-and-stick model of tartaric acid. C2 and C3 have a horizontal symmetry plane.

Some physical properties of the three stereoisomers are listed in the table. The (+)- and (−)-tartaric acids have identical melting points, solubilities, and densities, but they differ in the sign of their rotation of plane-polarized light. The meso isomer, by contrast, is diastereomeric with the (+) and (−) forms. It has no mirror-image relationship to (+)- and (−)-tartaric acids, is a different compound altogether, and thus has different physical properties.

Representation
Internal mirror test
Click HO, H or CO2H on either stereocenter in the 3‑D model — its mirror partner across the plane lights up.
Guided tour
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: The 3-D model's mirror plane is drawn as a large, strongly tilted parallelogram that extends well beyond the molecule and dominates the right side; in the source it is a thin, nearly edge-on pale band tucked between the two stereocenters.

The model's camera elevation/azimuth compresses the vertical C–C axis: the two gray stereocenter carbons nearly overlap and the light-blue stereocenter hydrogens are almost hidden, whereas the source shows a clearly vertical two-carbon backbone with both blue H atoms visible.

In the default Overlay mode the 2-D skeletal drawing is rendered at 0.6 opacity (washed-out grey lines and faded labels) instead of the crisp black bonds/solid lettering of the source; the model and the drawing also sit closer together so the 'Symmetry plane' text nearly touches the 3-D plane.

Substituent proportions in the model differ from the source: the OH oxygen/H and the carboxyl cluster are smaller relative to the plane and the C–H bonds are noticeably short, so the ball-and-stick arm lengths look cramped compared with the well-spread arms in the original.

The 2-D drawing uses a bold wedge to HO on both centers but a plain line to CO₂H, while the source's wedge/dash pattern around each carbon reads as a full tetrahedral set; the stereo notation is therefore slightly less explicit than the original.
evaluation.notes: Both panels of the source (flat stereo drawing + ball-and-stick meso tartaric acid with an internal mirror plane) are present with correct colors and labels, and the interaction set (representation toggle, mirror-pair picking, reflection animation, guided tour) is rich and conceptually on-point; the main weaknesses are an oversized, over-tilted symmetry plane, a compressed model view that hides the stereocenter hydrogens, and a washed-out 2-D drawing in the default overlay mode.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct (concept 5, interactivity 5); the issues are execution-level rendering details—oversized/over-tilted mirror plane, compressed camera hiding stereocenter hydrogens, washed-out 2-D overlay, and cramped bond lengths.

interactions.teaches: The same internal mirror plane can be found in the flat line drawing and in the real 3D geometry — the two depictions describe one molecule, not two arguments.
interactions.label: Representation

interactions.teaches: Every substituent on the top stereocenter has an exact mirror partner on the bottom one, so the two centers have opposite configurations and their handedness cancels.
Rotating the ball-and-stick model shows the mirror relationship holds in three dimensions, not just in the drawing's projection.
Reflecting the top half through the plane lands it exactly on the bottom half — the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image, i.e. meso and achiral despite two chirality centers.
interactions.label: Reflect top half through the plane

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Meso tartaric acid, HO2C–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–CO2H. World scale: central C–C bond 1.6 units, drawn vertically along +Y with the upper carbon at (0, 0.8, 0) and lower at (0, -0.8, 0). Symmetry plane is a horizontal parallelogram in the y=0 plane, ~5 units wide (X) × 2 units deep (Z), pale blue #b9dff5 at ~45% opacity, edges slightly darker; it is perpendicular to the C–C bond and extends beyond the molecule on both sides. Upper carbon substituents (bond length 1.1): OH oxygen up-left at (-0.9, 1.4, 0.15) with its hydroxyl H beyond at (-1.5, 1.05, 0.3); H (small, 0.45× radius) down-right toward viewer at (0.55, 0.45, 0.85); carboxyl carbon up-right at (0.95, 1.4, -0.1), branching to two oxygens at (1.9, 1.15, 0.1) and (0.95, 2.4, -0.3) plus a small acid H. discrepancies: In the source the 3-D model reads as two clearly stacked halves (upper set of substituents well above the plane, lower set well below); in the generated view the elevated camera plus the small C–C separation makes the two halves overlap almost on top of each other, obscuring the top/bottom mirror relationship.

The symmetry plane in the source is drawn nearly edge-on as a thin pale-blue band spanning the whole width of the molecule; here it is a small tilted parallelogram offset to the right that is partly hidden inside the ball cluster.
The 'Symmetry plane' label collides with the left edge of the 3-D model instead of sitting clearly in the gap between the drawing and the model as in the source.
In the source both stereocenter carbons are the same medium gray; in the render the lower carbon appears noticeably lighter/bluish than the upper one, weakening the mirror-symmetry impression.
The 2-D structural drawing is rendered smaller relative to the 3-D model than in the source, where the two panels are roughly comparable in visual weight.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and conceptually correct meso-tartaric-acid figure with both the 2-D drawing and ball-and-stick model, correct colors and a rich set of meaningful interactions (mode toggle, mirror-pair picking, fold slider, guided tour); the main weakness is the compressed/overlapping 3-D composition and a small, offset symmetry plane that makes the top/bottom mirror relationship less legible than in the source.
